title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (study_id=rX4f7-1). Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0000, 0.0058381985] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). The guarded pipeline invoked automated repair only three times. The preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was recorded in the preregistration but the archived confirmatory analysis executed and archived only the pooled paired analysis; H3 was therefore not executed as a confirmatory test and is reported here as an unperformed preregistered item and as a limitation. Under our synthetic corpus and validator configuration we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; all primary numbers, provider audits, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived to enable exact reproduction.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Systems and survey literature emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on the surrounding orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks syntactic and semantic constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules [3–6]. Despite conceptual support, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate per pair. The primary research question (from the preregistration) was: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation? Our principal contributions are (1) a preregistered experimental design and full execution artifacts (study_id = rX4f7-1); (2) a transparent, paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) artifact‑grounded accounting that documents why repair was rarely invoked and why the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory comparison (H3) was not produced in the archived confirmatory outputs. The manuscript explicitly reports that H3 was preregistered but not executed as a confirmatory test; the pooled analysis is the archived confirmatory outcome.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers position LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasize that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [1–3]. Generate–validate‑repair patterns appear across NL→formal translation, topology compilation, and configuration remediation prototypes; these works demonstrate feasibility but also show sensitivity to verifier rule‑sets, dataset construction choices, and task difficulty [4–9]. Failure‑mode analyses (hallucination, semantic/unit errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, prompt‑injection) motivate verifier scaffolding but leave open the operational question of how much verifier assistance improves end‑to‑end, rollback‑aware correctness in paired comparisons [10–14]. NetOpsTraceBench was designed to make such dependencies observable by freezing seeds, validator rules, and binary success criteria and archiving full traces.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study preregistration (NetOpsTraceBench, rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) froze confirmatory hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination thresholds, seeds, stopping rules, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration targeted 1,200 paired tasks (edge=600, core=600) and an MDE of 5 percentage points (α=0.05, power=0.8) under assumed baseline ≈0.70.

Task corpus, validator and pipelines: The benchmark used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to create 1,200 intent→config tasks with structured payloads (initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, declared difficulty). Per preregistration, generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false): each task produced one shared initial candidate that both conditions received. The requested model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json records requested_model=gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens=1500). The guarded pipeline routed the shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0); if rejected the pipeline could invoke at most one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The baseline pipeline recorded the same shared initial candidate and proceeded to deterministic parsing and emulator preflight checks without repair. Contamination checks, exclusion rules, and the missingness plan were applied deterministically as preregistered.

Analytic scope and preregistered but unexecuted H3: The preregistration included an exploratory/confirmatory topology‑cluster breakdown hypothesis (H3). The archived confirmatory analysis executed and produced only the pooled paired binary analysis (complete_pair_count = 1,199) and associated artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). No archived per‑cluster confirmatory contingency tables or per‑cluster inference outputs were produced by the confirmatory analysis executor; therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory inference and is reported here as an unperformed preregistered item. This manuscript corrects prior wording that implied H3 was executed and treats per‑cluster inference as a limitation and a target for future sensitivity analyses. The pooled analysis and all primary numbers are archived and cited below.

Rationale for shared_initial_candidate design: The shared initial candidate design isolates verifier and repair effects by removing variability from independent per‑condition generation. This choice reduces confounding caused by generation stochasticity and clarifies whether repairs triggered by the verifier (rather than different initial samples) drive improvements. As archived (execution/execution_manifest.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json), stage_counts show shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3, confirming that a single initial candidate per task was used and that most guarded episodes accepted the initial candidate without repair.
sections.results:
Execution and pair accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1) and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 1,200, repair: 3} (deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution/execution_manifest.json). Repair was therefore invoked in only three episodes.

Primary pooled outcomes: The pooled paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. From these counts baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076) and guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0). The observed paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446.

Confirmatory inference and uncertainty: The archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs (n10 = 3, n01 = 0), yielding p = 0.25 (analysis/results.json). A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. The small number of discordant pairs produces limited inferential resolution for small absolute effects; the observed near‑ceiling baseline reduces headroom for measurable gains relative to the preregistered MDE.

Missingness, exclusions, and contamination: The preregistered deterministic exclusions were not triggered for contamination (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). The missingness summary (analysis/missingness_summary.csv) records complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. The analysis used the preregistered complete_pair_primary treatment (exclude deterministically excluded pairs). The single dropped pair reduced the planned 1,200 pairs to 1,199 complete pairs.

Representative validator traces and repair diagnostics: Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json, task-000002-*.json, task-000003-*.json) show that validation_after.valid = true in the vast majority of episodes and repair_applied = false for most cases. Task manifests include declared difficulty levels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard"); even higher‑difficulty tasks often produced validator‑acceptable initial candidates under the chosen generator and validator settings. These artifact traces support the operational interpretation that the deterministic task generator and validator configuration produced many initial candidates that already satisfied intent constraints, limiting opportunities for repair to alter the pooled binary outcome.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The pooled confirmatory evidence shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under these corpus and validator settings (McNemar p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded explanations are supported by archived logs. First, the baseline one‑shot success was near ceiling (≈99.75%), leaving little absolute headroom for improvement; the preregistered power analysis targeted a 5 percentage‑point MDE and therefore the run was underpowered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect. Second, the shared_initial_candidate design and deterministic task generator produced initial candidates that typically satisfied the validator (stage_counts: repair = 3), so the verifier rarely exercised its repair capability.

Implications for benchmark design and verifier evaluation: Our results imply that a verifier’s measurable benefit on a binary success metric depends critically on task corpus difficulty, task ambiguity/adversariality, and verifier strictness. When initial generation already meets deterministic verifier criteria for common, well‑specified tasks, generate–validate–repair pipelines will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To reveal verifier value, future studies should (a) increase task ambiguity or adversarial edge cases, (b) vary verifier strictness and rule sets, (c) perform per‑cluster (topology) confirmatory analyses as preregistered, and (d) test multiple LLM families.

Threats to validity and scope: Internal validity is strong because seeds, generator, validator, and exclusion rules were deterministic and archived. Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) maps to operationally meaningful correctness in production. External validity is limited: a single requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was exercised, tasks were synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies or complex transient dynamics. Importantly, the preregistered H3 per‑topology confirmatory test was not executed and per‑cluster confirmatory inference is therefore not available in the archived confirmatory outputs; this absence constrains claims about topology‑specific consistency and is reported here as an explicit limitation rather than omitted provenance.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench provides an artifact‑rich, preregistered, paired evaluation comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines. Under the synthetic, deterministic task corpus and validator configuration used here and with gpt-5-mini as requested, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%); the guarded pipeline improved absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) but this small gain is not statistically significant (McNemar p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Repair was invoked only three times, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate design and the task/validator choices. The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory analysis (H3) was not executed and hence is not reported as a confirmed result; future work should perform the per‑cluster confirmatory comparisons and explore more adversarial, ambiguous corpora and multiple model families. All raw outputs, validator traces, provider audits, and analysis code are archived to permit exact reproduction and follow‑up sensitivity studies.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary; this deviation is documented in archived analysis artifacts.

Unexecuted preregistered item (H3): The preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory comparison (edge vs core) was not executed as a confirmatory analysis in the archived outputs and therefore per‑cluster confirmatory inference is not available in this report.
